intro: Some of the questions people ask most about Israel are bitterly contested. This section sets out each one the same way: what is claimed, what the record shows, where the real disagreement lies, what Israel and its defenders answer, and where to read more on every side. Dates and sources are shown so you can check them.

topics.title: Why did about 700,000 Palestinians leave in 1948, and may they return?
topics.brief: Roughly 700,000 Arabs left or were driven from the territory that became Israel during the war of 1947 to 1949, and Israel did not let them return. Historians agree on those facts. They disagree on how much was flight from war, how much was expulsion, and whether any plan lay behind it.
claim: Palestinians call 1948 the Nakba, the catastrophe. They say their communities were deliberately emptied, villages were destroyed, and the refugees were barred from coming home.

Historians such as Ilan Pappe argue that the Zionist leadership carried out a planned ethnic cleansing, pointing to Plan Dalet of March 1948 and to expulsions in places such as Lydda and Ramle in July 1948.
record: Between about 700,000 and 750,000 Arabs left or were expelled from the territory that became Israel, and hundreds of villages were emptied.
Israel did not allow the refugees back after the 1949 armistice agreements, and later laws barred the return of absentees.

UN General Assembly Resolution 194 of December 1948 said refugees who wished to return and live in peace should be allowed to do so at the earliest practicable date, with compensation for the rest. It is a recommendation and not a binding order.
Around 160,000 Arabs stayed and became Israeli citizens. Roughly 850,000 Jews left or were forced out of Arab states and Iran in the decades that followed.
critics: There were many expulsions, and Israel's refusal to allow return made the displacement permanent.
Plan Dalet and military orders show intent to clear territory, even if no single written order covers every case.
defenders: The war began when Arab leaders rejected the November 1947 partition plan and Arab armies invaded in May 1948.
The historian Benny Morris, who documented expulsions in detail, found that most Arabs left because of the war and fear and that no master plan for expulsion existed.
Some Arab leaders urged civilians to leave, a claim historians dispute for most places.
A mass return would end the Jewish majority of the only Jewish state, and the Jewish refugees from Arab lands were never compensated either.
dates: UN General Assembly votes to partition Mandatory Palestine.
Plan Dalet is drawn up by the Haganah.
Deir Yassin, where Irgun and Lehi fighters killed villagers, spreads fear across the country.
Israel declares independence and Arab armies invade.
Lydda and Ramle are taken and most of their residents leave or are forced out.
Armistice agreements end the fighting. Israel refuses return.
voices: Palestinian nationalism and the refugee question
Explains the 1948 war and its aftermath
sources: Benny Morris, The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited (2004)
Israeli historian, documents expulsions and finds no master plan
Ilan Pappe, The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine (2006)
Rashid Khalidi, The Hundred Years' War on Palestine (2020)
Argues that the flight was largely the result of Arab choices
Neutral overview with the main sources

topics.title: Is Israel a settler-colonial state?
topics.brief: This is mainly a dispute among scholars about which framework fits best. It is not something a court has decided. Both sides can point to real history, so the answer turns on how one defines colonialism and indigeneity.
claim: Critics argue that Zionism brought European Jews to settle a land already inhabited by Arabs, with the backing of an imperial power, Britain, and that the Palestinians were displaced as a result.

They note that early Zionists used the word colonization themselves, as in the Jewish Colonization Association, and that Ze'ev Jabotinsky's 1923 essay The Iron Wall was open about the conflict that settlement would cause.
record: Early Zionist institutions did use the vocabulary of colonization before the 1940s.
Jews have lived in the land continuously, and Jewish prayer has faced Jerusalem for over two thousand years. Large-scale modern immigration began in the 1880s.
About half of Israel's Jewish population descends from Jews who lived in Middle Eastern and North African countries, and many arrived as refugees.
Britain's role was mixed. It issued the Balfour Declaration in 1917 and then restricted Jewish immigration in the 1939 White Paper, and Zionist groups fought British rule.
critics: The pattern of land purchase, settlement and displacement fits the settler-colonial model developed by scholars such as Patrick Wolfe.
A people's historical tie to a land does not remove the claims of those who lived there for centuries.
defenders: Jews are an indigenous people returning to their ancestral homeland, and the movement was a national liberation movement rather than an imperial one.
There was no mother country that sent the settlers. Most Jewish immigrants were refugees from persecution in Europe and the Middle East.
The framework erases Jewish history and treats Israel as foreign in the one place where Jewish identity was formed.
dates: First Aliyah of Zionist pioneers begins.
First Zionist Congress meets in Basel.
British White Paper restricts Jewish immigration.
voices: Argues Zionism is a return and not a colonial project
sources: Rashid Khalidi, The Hundred Years' War on Palestine (2020)
A Zionist leader on colonization and Arab opposition
Gershon Shafir, Land, Labor and the Origins of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict
Scholarly study of the early settlements

topics.title: Are Israel's West Bank settlements legal?
topics.brief: Most governments and the International Court of Justice say the settlements violate international law. Israel rejects that view and argues that the West Bank is disputed and not occupied sovereign territory. The legal question is the clearest example on this list of a dispute where the main authorities side with one position.
claim: Critics say that moving civilians into occupied territory violates Article 49(6) of the Fourth Geneva Convention, and that settlements take land and block a Palestinian state.
They also point to settler violence and to the growth of outposts that are illegal even under Israeli law.
record: In its 2004 advisory opinion on the separation barrier, the ICJ said the settlements were established in breach of international law.
UN Security Council Resolution 2334 of December 2016 said the settlements have no legal validity. The United States abstained.
On 19 July 2024 the ICJ issued an advisory opinion saying Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory is unlawful and that Israel should end it and evacuate settlers.
There are roughly half a million Israeli settlers in the West Bank and over 200,000 more in East Jerusalem. Figures vary by source.
critics: The Geneva Convention bans an occupier from transferring its own population into occupied land, and Israel's settlement policy does exactly that.
Settlements fragment the West Bank and make a contiguous Palestinian state hard to build.
defenders: Article 49(6) was written to bar forced transfers such as those Nazi Germany carried out. Israelis moved voluntarily.
Jordan held the West Bank from 1948 to 1967 without wide international recognition, so there was no prior legitimate sovereign. The territory is disputed, to be settled by negotiation.
The Jewish connection to Judea and Samaria goes back thousands of years, and the League of Nations mandate recognized Jewish rights there.
Israel removed all settlements from Gaza in 2005 and from parts of the northern West Bank, which shows they are negotiable.
dates: Israel takes the West Bank in the Six-Day War.
Oslo Accords divide the West Bank into Areas A, B and C.
ICJ advisory opinion on the separation barrier.
Israel withdraws from Gaza and four northern West Bank settlements.
ICJ advisory opinion on the occupation.
sources: ICJ: Advisory opinion on the occupied Palestinian territory (case 186)
Neutral overview of law, numbers and history
Levy Report (2012), Israeli Ministry of Justice committee
The Israeli government committee that argued the settlements are lawful
B'Tselem and Peace Now settlement monitoring
Israeli organizations that track and oppose the settlements

topics.title: Is Israel an apartheid state?
topics.brief: Several major human rights groups say yes, and Israel and its defenders strongly deny it. The disagreement rests on whether Israel and the West Bank should be judged as one system, and on whether discrimination alone, or only an intent to dominate one racial group, defines apartheid.
claim: B'Tselem (January 2021), Human Rights Watch (April 2021) and Amnesty International (February 2022) concluded that Israel maintains a system of domination over Palestinians that meets the legal definition of apartheid.
They argue that Palestinians in the West Bank live under military law while nearby settlers live under civil law, and that Palestinian citizens of Israel face unequal treatment in land and housing.
record: Apartheid is a crime against humanity under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court and under the Apartheid Convention.

In its July 2024 advisory opinion the ICJ found that Israel's policies in the occupied territory breach Article 3 of the Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which bans racial segregation and apartheid, but it did not rule on which of the two applies.
About a fifth of Israel's citizens are Arab. They vote, sit in the Knesset and serve on the Supreme Court, and Israel's 2018 Nation-State Law was criticized as relegating them.
critics: Seen as a single regime controlling the whole territory from the river to the sea, Israel gives different rights to different groups.
Separate legal systems in the West Bank, land policies and the Nation-State Law show systematic discrimination.
defenders: Israeli Arabs are full citizens with the vote. Apartheid in South Africa denied Black citizens political rights altogether.
The West Bank is a separate territory under occupation and the Palestinian Authority governs most Palestinians there. The conflict is over national claims, not race.
Apartheid requires an intent to maintain racial domination. Security barriers followed terror attacks and negotiation offers, and not a racial plan.
dates: UN Apartheid Convention opens for signature.
ICJ advisory opinion refers to CERD Article 3.
sources: Human Rights Watch: A Threshold Crossed (2021)
Amnesty International: Israel's Apartheid Against Palestinians (2022)
Wikipedia: Israel and the apartheid analogy
Neutral overview with sources on all sides
Critic of the NGOs behind the reports

topics.title: Is Israel committing genocide in Gaza?
topics.brief: A UN commission, Amnesty International and a number of scholars say yes. Israel says no and points to its aim of defeating Hamas after the attack of 7 October 2023. The International Court of Justice has not ruled. It has only found a plausible risk and ordered precautions, and its final judgment is years away.
claim: South Africa filed a case at the ICJ in December 2023 alleging that Israel violates the Genocide Convention.

On 16 September 2025 the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza and that senior officials incited it. Amnesty International reached a similar finding in December 2024.

These bodies cite mass killing, the siege and starvation, the destruction of health and education systems, and statements by Israeli officials as evidence of intent to destroy Palestinians as a group.
record: The Genocide Convention requires specific acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group in whole or in part. Intent is the hardest element to prove.

On 26 January 2024 the ICJ found that the rights South Africa claimed were plausible and ordered Israel to prevent genocidal acts and allow aid. It did not decide whether genocide has occurred, and it did not order a ceasefire.

Israel filed its Counter-Memorial in March 2026 and objects to the court's jurisdiction. In June 2026 the court set 22 November 2027 for South Africa's Reply and 22 May 2029 for Israel's Rejoinder. No hearing date has been set.
The commission's findings are not a court judgment. Israel did not cooperate with it. Gaza's casualty figures come from the Hamas-run health ministry, which UN agencies use and Israel questions.
critics: The pattern of conduct, the blockade and statements by ministers show intent beyond the aim of defeating Hamas.
The scale of civilian death and destruction is consistent with an intent to destroy the group, and a number of genocide scholars have said so.
defenders: Israel went to war after Hamas killed about 1,200 people on 7 October 2023 and took about 250 hostages. Its stated aim is to dismantle Hamas and free the hostages.
Genocide requires intent to destroy a people. Israel warned civilians, evacuated areas, let in aid and has a civilian population in Gaza that kept growing before the war.

Hamas fights from civilian areas and has said it would repeat the attack, which complicates casualty ratios. Military analysts such as John Spencer argue the civilian-to-combatant ratio is low for urban war.
Israel argues that statements cited as proof of intent came from individual officials and do not reflect the military's operational orders.
dates: South Africa files its case at the ICJ.
UN Commission of Inquiry finds genocide.
sources: UN Commission of Inquiry, report of 16 September 2025
Primary source for the genocide finding
Wikipedia: South Africa v. Israel (Genocide Convention)
Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (1948)
Raphael Lemkin, Axis Rule in Occupied Europe (1944)
The book where the word genocide was coined

topics.title: Has Israel committed war crimes in Gaza?
topics.brief: The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Gallant, and Israel rejects the court's jurisdiction. The same court issued a warrant for a Hamas leader for the 7 October attack. Allegations are numerous and Israel says its military investigates them.
claim: On 21 November 2024 the ICC's Pre-Trial Chamber issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant for the war crime of starvation as a method of warfare and for crimes against humanity including murder and persecution.
Human rights groups have alleged attacks on aid convoys, hospitals and civilian homes, and the killing of aid workers.
record: Israel is not a member of the ICC, but the Palestinian territories accepted its jurisdiction in 2015. Israel disputes that Palestine qualifies as a state.
The court also issued a warrant for Hamas military chief Mohammed Deif, which was later withdrawn after Israel said it had killed him.

Israel challenged the court's jurisdiction. In April 2025 the Appeals Chamber ordered the lower chamber to review that challenge again. The court refused to suspend the warrants in July 2025 and rejected a further appeal in October 2025. As of the latest reports found, the jurisdiction question remains pending.
Hamas and other groups are accused of war crimes for the 7 October attack, the taking of hostages and the use of civilian areas for military purposes.
critics: Israel's own investigations rarely lead to indictments, so international courts must step in.
Restrictions on aid and strikes on civilian sites amount to violations of the laws of war.
defenders: The ICC lacks jurisdiction because Israel is not a party and Palestine is not a sovereign state. Israel has its own independent system, led by the Military Advocate General.
The warrants equate a democracy defending itself with the leaders of a terror group.
Hamas operates from hospitals, schools and tunnels, which turns those sites into legitimate targets under the laws of war when they are used for military purposes.
Israel says it takes precautions that other armies do not, including warnings and evacuation routes.
dates: ICC issues warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant.
Appeals Chamber sends the jurisdiction challenge back for review.
ICC refuses to suspend the warrants.
voices: British army veteran on war law
sources: ICC: Situation in the State of Palestine
B'Tselem and Yesh Din on investigations
Israeli organizations on how rarely soldiers are prosecuted
Israeli government and IDF statements on investigations
The IDF Military Advocate General's reports
Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocol I

topics.title: Was there famine in Gaza, and who is responsible?
topics.brief: The UN-backed food security monitor declared famine in part of Gaza in August 2025, and said in December 2025 that no area remained in famine after the October ceasefire. Israel disputes the finding and blames Hamas for diverting aid. The key facts are the dates of closure and reopening of crossings.
claim: UN agencies and aid groups say that Israel's restrictions on food and aid caused severe hunger and in places famine.
The ICC warrants allege starvation as a method of warfare.
record: Israel closed the crossings to goods in early March 2025 and the restriction lasted for about eleven weeks.
On 22 August 2025 the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) confirmed famine in Gaza Governorate, affecting about 514,000 people.

After the 10 October 2025 ceasefire improved access, the IPC said on 19 December 2025 that no area was classified as famine. It warned that conditions remained fragile and that renewed fighting could bring the risk back.
In 2025 a new aid mechanism backed by the United States and Israel, the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, began operating and drew criticism from the UN and aid groups.
critics: Israel controls the crossings, so restrictions on entry are the main cause of shortages.
Shooting incidents near aid sites and delays at crossings show that the system failed civilians.
defenders: Hamas stole and taxed aid and Israel allowed in large volumes of food, which the Israeli agency COGAT counts and publishes.
The IPC relied on data from sources Israel says were incomplete or came from Hamas-run sources, and Israel rejected the famine finding.
The closure in March 2025 was meant to pressure Hamas to free hostages after the first ceasefire ended.
dates: Partial reopening and launch of the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation.
IPC confirms famine in Gaza Governorate.
IPC says no area is in famine.
sources: Primary source for the famine classifications
Israeli defense body that coordinates aid and publishes truck counts
UN OCHA: Humanitarian situation updates for Gaza

topics.title: Is the Gaza blockade legal, and is Gaza still occupied?
topics.brief: Israel and Egypt have restricted goods and movement into Gaza since Hamas took power in 2007. The legal questions are whether Israel still occupies Gaza after leaving in 2005, and whether a blockade is lawful or collective punishment.
claim: Critics, including the Red Cross, say the closure is collective punishment of civilians and that Israel still controls Gaza's borders, airspace and coast, so it remains responsible as an occupier.
The ICJ's 2024 advisory opinion said Israel's obligations in Gaza continue to the extent it exercises effective control.
record: Israel withdrew all troops and settlers from Gaza in 2005.
Hamas won legislative elections in 2006 and took over Gaza by force in June 2007. Israel and Egypt then tightened restrictions.
A UN Secretary-General panel, the Palmer Report of 2011, found that Israel's naval blockade was a legal security measure, while criticizing the Mavi Marmara raid of 2010 as excessive.
Egypt also restricts the Rafah crossing, which is often left out of the debate.
critics: Restricting almost all exports, medicine and building materials harms ordinary people far beyond any security need.
Control of the territory's borders amounts to occupation in practice.
defenders: After the withdrawal Gaza had its own government and Hamas used the territory to fire rockets and dig attack tunnels. A blockade to stop weapons is lawful.
Egypt shares the border and also closes it, so the cause is Hamas rule and not Israeli policy alone.
Hamas diverted cement and other dual-use goods to build tunnels, which is why restrictions on some materials remained.
sources: Palmer Report (2011), UN Secretary-General's Panel of Inquiry
Primary document on the legality of the blockade
Wikipedia: Blockade of the Gaza Strip

topics.title: What happened in Jenin in April 2002?
topics.brief: Early reports spoke of a massacre of hundreds. A later UN report and investigations by Human Rights Watch found no massacre, but did find serious abuses. The case is a lesson in how fast claims spread and why dated, checked sources matter.
claim: During Operation Defensive Shield, Palestinian officials and some media said Israeli forces massacred hundreds of civilians in the Jenin refugee camp.
Figures of 500 or more dead were repeated in the first days.
record: The UN Secretary-General's report of August 2002 put the Palestinian death toll at about 52, with 23 Israeli soldiers killed, and did not find a massacre.
Human Rights Watch found no massacre but documented serious violations that may amount to war crimes, including the use of civilians as human shields and unlawful killings.
Amnesty International likewise documented possible war crimes. Israel refused to allow a full UN fact-finding team in and the mission was cancelled.
critics: Israel blocked an independent inquiry and the camp was sealed for days, so the full story was hard to check.
Rights groups still found abuses that deserved prosecution.
defenders: The massacre claim collapsed under later evidence, which shows how quickly false numbers spread.
The battle followed the Passover massacre in Netanya and a wave of suicide bombings, and the camp was a base for attackers.
Israel sent soldiers into the camp, instead of bombing from the air, to reduce civilian deaths, and paid a high price for that choice.
dates: Operation Defensive Shield and the Battle of Jenin.
voices: British army officer on the battle
sources: Human Rights Watch: Jenin, IDF Military Operations (May 2002)
Report that found abuses and no massacre

topics.title: Where is the line between criticizing Israel and antisemitism?
topics.brief: Almost everyone agrees that criticizing Israeli policy is not antisemitic and that hatred of Jews is. The dispute is over the middle ground, especially denying the Jewish people's right to a state, and whether definitions such as the IHRA's protect Jews or chill legitimate speech.
claim: Defenders of the IHRA working definition, adopted in 2016, say that denying Jews the right to self-determination, applying double standards to Israel and using classic antisemitic images against it are forms of antisemitism.
Critics say the definition is used to silence criticism of Israel and to equate anti-Zionism with hatred of Jews.
record: UN General Assembly Resolution 3379 of 1975 declared that Zionism is a form of racism. The Assembly revoked it on 16 December 1991.
The IHRA working definition has been adopted by many governments and universities. Its authors have said it was not meant to be a legal speech code.
In March 2021 a group of scholars issued the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism as an alternative that separates harsh criticism of Israel from antisemitism.
Reported antisemitic incidents rose sharply in many countries after 7 October 2023, according to monitoring groups such as the ADL.
critics: Labeling political criticism as antisemitism harms free speech, and Jews themselves disagree about Zionism.
The IHRA examples are too broad and are used by governments to restrict protest.
defenders: Zionism is the belief that the Jewish people have a right to a state, and surveys show that most Jews feel attached to Israel.
Denying that right to Jews alone, while accepting national movements for every other people, is a double standard.
Protests that target Jewish students and institutions, and chants that call for Israel's elimination, go beyond policy criticism.
dates: Antisemitic incidents rise worldwide after 7 October.
sources: Wikipedia: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 3379
